https://whbl.com/2026/07/24/france-reque.text: Sign In Search NEWS WEATHER EVENTS OBITUARIES CLOSINGS MORE AGRICULTURE BLOGS LOCAL SPORTS ON AIR PODCASTS France orders total evacuation of Cap Ferret peninsula as wildfires rage By Thomson Reuters Jul 24, 2026 | 12:10 AM By Stephane Mahe LEGE-CAP FERRET, France, July 24 (Reuters) – French authorities ordered on Friday the total evacuation of the Cap Ferret peninsula, a tourism hotspot on the Atlantic Coast, sending boats to remove people from an area threatened by ​a major wildfire. The order for a total evacuation of the area, which is ‌home to many valuable properties and is currently full of tourists enjoying their summer vacations in camp sites and rental homes, underlined the severity of the fire. French President Emmanuel Macron said he had requested help from the European Union as the country’s battle against wildfires intensifies. “France has requested the activation of the ‌European ​Union’s civil protection mechanism. We will soon be able to ⁠count on reinforcements from two ⁠Croatian Canadair aircraft, two Portuguese Air Tractor planes, as well as two heavy Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia,” wrote Macron on X on Friday. Sophie Brocas, the prefect for the Nouvelle Aquitaine region, said on Friday that evacuees from ​the Cap Ferret peninsula could leave from piers in four villages in the area between 7 a.m. and 10 a.m. local time (0500 GMT and 0800 GMT). All those still ⁠present in those villages must leave either on the ⁠boats or by the only road linking the area with the ​mainland, she added. The fire has already devastated 8,700 hectares and is still raging. FRANCE HARD HIT BY ​THIS SUMMER’S HEATWAVES Across Europe, three heatwaves in succession this season have intensified ‌drought, strained water supplies and left vegetation tinder-dry, helping wildfires scorch more land already this year than the annual average of the past two decades. The heat has also been blamed for thousands of deaths. France has been particularly hard hit, with the intense heat pressuring ⁠its capacity to handle the situation. “Our security forces are engaged in a genuine battle against the wildfires,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Thursday evening. “The nation stands with you.” The pressure on ⁠fire departments in southwestern France ‌has been increased by another wildfire that began on Thursday afternoon ⁠near Biscarosse, just 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Cap Ferret. That fire, ​which ‌is still not under control, has devastated 2,500 hectares, the prefect ​for the ⁠Landes area, Gilles Clavreul, said in a statement. “Winds are blowing, and the situation remains highly dynamic and unfavourable,” he said. More than 23,000 people were evacuated from the Biscarosse district, mainly in campsites and homes and a children’s summer camp and a residential care home for the elderly were also evacuated. He asked farmers to contribute with water tanks. (Reporting by Camille Raynaud and Inti ​LandauroEditing by Gareth Jones) Comments Leave a Reply Cancel reply You must be logged in to post a comment. https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/wea.text: For years, working abroad meant securing a foreign job or investing heavily through a golden visa programme. Today, digital nomad visas offer a new route, allowing professionals to live overseas while working remotely for employers or clients elsewhere. With no multi-crore investment requirement and remote work on the rise, they are attracting Indian software professionals, consultants, founders and content creators seeking global mobility without changing careers. Industry experts say enquiries from Indians have surged over the past three years, reflecting the shift towards flexible work and the growing appeal of countries offering a better quality of life.New mobilityA digital nomad visa is a residence permit that allows an individual to legally stay in a foreign country while earning income from an employer or clients located outside that country. Unlike traditional work visas such as the H-1B in the US, it is not tied to sponsorship by a local employer.âIt provides legal clarity to work remotely, longer stays than tourist visas, access to local services and, in some countries, simplified tax treatment or pathways to residency,â says Andri Boiko, Founder and Global CEO, GARANT IN.Varun Singh, Managing Director, XIPHIAS Immigration, calls digital nomad visas âone of the biggest shifts in global mobility over the past decadeâ. He says they allow professionals to experience living abroad without changing employers while enabling host countries to attract skilled individuals who contribute to the local economy without competing for local jobs.ALSO READ | Foreign universities in India: Should you choose an Indian campus over studying abroad? Know the pros & consOne limitation is that these visas generally donât allow local employment, requiring holders to earn foreign income. Those wanting local jobs usually need a work visa. Spain is an exception, allowing up to 20% of the main applicantâs income from local clients, while spouses can work without such restrictions.Whatâs a digital nomad visaA residence permit that lets you live in another country while working remotely for an employer or clients based outside that country. It is designed for remote workers, not people seeking local employment. It allows:Work for a foreign employer/clientNo local job sponsorship neededTemporary residenceUsually cannot take local jobsRemote work or freelancingBest suited forSoftware professionalsConsultantsContent creatorsFreelancersStartup foundersNot meant forPeople seeking local employmentThose without a stable remote incomeWhy now?The primary reason for the rise in these visas is the mainstream acceptance of remote work following the Covid-19 pandemic. âRemote work moved from a niche idea to a mainstream way of working after the pandemic, and governments quickly saw the economic upside of attracting remote earners,â says Boiko. He notes that these professionals spend on housing, food, transport and leisure without competing for local jobs, making them attractive for governments. Estoniaâs launch of the first dedicated digital nomad visa in 2020 encouraged other countries to introduce similar programmes.ALSO READ | India visa and passport services disrupted in Australia after Delhi High Court scraps government tenderSingh says professionals are no longer choosing countries only for career opportunities. Lifestyle, safety, healthcare, infrastructure and international mobility have become equally important considerations. Entrepreneurs also see overseas residence as a way to expand globally and access new clients and investors. While favourable tax regimes matter, he cautions that a visa by itself does not change tax residency.Both experts say demand from India has accelerated sharply since 2023. Boiko says software and IT professionals remain the largest applicant group, followed by consultants and freelancers, while startup founders and content creators are emerging as fast-growing segments. Investors and retirees, on the other hand, usually prefer golden visas because those programmes are investment-led.Singh says his firm has seen enquiries rise significantly over the last three years. Initially dominated by software professionals and freelancers, interest has broadened to include startup founders, senior corporate executives, consultants, digital creators, architects, designers, financial consultants and online educators. âMany of these professionals are not looking to permanently relocate. Instead, they want international exposure while maintaining their existing careers and income sources,â he says.Top destinationsSpain has emerged as the top choice for many Indians. Boiko says its relatively low income threshold, favourable tax regime, Schengen access and flexible work rules make it more attractive than rivals. Portugal, Greece, Estonia, Malta and Dubai are also popular.ALSO READ | Dubai Residential Visa: You no longer need minimum 7.5 lakh Dirhams to buy a property, Dubai Land Department makes Visa rules easierSingh says the UAE remains a top choice too due to its zero personal income tax, strong infrastructure and large Indian community. Spain and Portugal offer a European lifestyle and long-term residency prospects, while Greece and Croatia provide lower living costs. Spain grants an initial entry visa valid for up to a year. Once you arrive in Spain, you can transition or renew this into a digital nomad residence authorisation that can last up to three years, while Portugal provides a four-month entry visa followed by a two-year permit. Greece issues a one-year visa, convertible to a two-year renewable permit All three can lead to permanent residency after five years, subject to eligibility. Applicants typically need stable overseas income, work contracts, health insurance, sufficient funds and a clean record; some countries require employer approval for overseas remote work. Including visa, insurance, documentation and advisory costs, expenses can range from Rs.1.5 lakh to Rs.8 lakh; for Spain, itâs Rs.9 lakh and for Portugal, Rs.8 lakh.Tax mattersThis is where it can get challenging. âMany people assume that obtaining a foreign visa automatically changes their tax residency. That is not the case,â says Singh.Under the Income Tax Act, residency status hinges mainly on how many days you spend in India physically during a financial year, with extra rules for high earners. Time spent abroad on a digital nomad visa can push someone into Non-Resident or RNOR (Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident) status â which changes whether their worldwide income stays taxable in India. The Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) rules and Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) provisions apply on top of this. âTax treatment usually follows where the work is physically performed, not where the pay cheque originates,â says Boiko.For salaried employees, overseas remote work may also require employer approval, as it can raise permanent-establishment concerns for the Indian company. âSome Indian companies are cautious about signing off on this,â Boiko notes.Challenges aheadWhile immigration itself may be straightforward, settling into another country often presents practical hurdles. Both experts identify taxation, banking, insurance, housing, employer compliance and understanding local regulations as the biggest challenges. Salaried employees may also need explicit permission from their employers, who could face tax or compliance issues arising from overseas remote work.Another important consideration is the long-term objective. Some countries, including Spain and Portugal, offer pathways to permanent residency after several years of legal residence, while others treat digital nomad visas as purely temporary arrangements with no route to settlement.For professionals with stable remote income, digital nomad visas offer an accessible alternative to golden visas. Instead of committing crores towards investment-linked residency, they allow individuals to test life abroad while continuing their careers. But experts caution these visas are not simply about working from a beach. Tax planning, employer consent, compliance and long-term immigration goals require careful consideration.

Photograph: PA Portsmouth Hundreds of far-right protesters descend on Portsmouth after small boat arrival Influencer livestreams event calling for men to travel to port to block coaches carrying asylum seekers from leaving Diane Taylor and Charlie Moloney Sun 6 Sep 2026 21.33 EDT First published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 17.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hundreds of far-right activists have descended on Portsmouth , where a small boat with 140 asylum seekers on board was intercepted heading towards the Portsmouth coast. The vessel’s arrival sparked a major response with a helicopter, an aeroplane and lifeboats sent to the scene. It is thought to be the first time such a large boat containing asylum seekers has been brought to Portsmouth and the first time a large group of anti-migrant protesters have tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed. The protesters blocked roads for hours and vowed to stay all night to prevent the new arrivals from being taken to a processing centre. It is the second major anti-migrant protest of the weekend. Many of those at Portsmouth were dressed in all black and wore face masks, similar to those who attended a rally that blocked roads in Dover on Saturday. One witness who was not involved in the protest said on Sunday night: “The atmosphere here is still very tense. The coaches carrying asylum seekers have still not left. About 25-30% of the far-right protesters are wearing balaclavas and many are wearing black. Two police cars had their windscreens smashed by protesters. At one point they broke through the police cordon.” View image in fullscreen Police at the site of a far-right protest in Portsmouth on Sunday night, following the arrival of a migrant boat. Photograph: Supplied The boat’s occupants were brought to shore in the maritime city and the Home Office’s plan was to take them to Manston, outside Ramsgate in Kent, where small boat arrivals are processed. However, videos circulating on social media showed large groups of protesters close to the coaches that were to be used, with some blocking vehicles carrying asylum seekers from leaving. Hampshire police urged people to avoid the area, and said a dispersal order was in place. The government has condemned what it described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesters. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.” In a livestream from the scene, Daniel Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo – a former bodyguard of the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – encouraged viewers to travel to Portsmouth to join the protest. View image in fullscreen Damage to the windscreen of a police car at the site of a far-right protest in Portsmouth on Sunday night, following the arrival of a migrant boat. Photograph: Supplied Thomas has recently established Patriot Platform which blocked part of port of Dover on Saturday. He previously launched Operation Overlord which planned to send far-right activists to France to “stop the boats”. He and his supporters filmed themselves slashing abandoned dinghies on a French beach. The french authorities subsequently banned him from France. Small boat crossings so far this year have reduced by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. While the Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model, their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats such as the one that arrived on Sunday evening from different parts of the coast, much further from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous. Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI boats on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore in Dover. The Maritime and Coastguard Agency said it was alerted on Sunday to a small boat heading towards the Hampshire coast. The coastguard sent lifeboats, a helicopter, an aeroplane and rescue teams to the area, a spokesperson said. “Border Force, Border Security Command, Hampshire police and south central ambulance service were also sent,” they said. View image in fullscreen About 140 migrants arrive in Portsmouth, Hampshire, after being transferred from a single dinghy south of the Isle of Wight in the English Channel by two RNLI lifeboats. Photograph: Paul Jacobs/pictureexclusive.com Saturday’s Port of Dover rally was criticised by politicians from all parties, with questions expected to be raised on Monday about whether Kent police were prepared for it. There could be similar criticism of Hampshire police. The Dover demonstrations brought traffic on routes to the UK’s busiest international ferry and passenger port to a halt, delaying some ferry services and blocking major roads, but there were no arrests. The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, criticised the demonstrations, which saw protesters march through Dover chanting “Whose streets? Our streets” and “Stop the boats”. Reynolds told Sky News he condemned the behaviour and the disruption it caused, adding: “Peaceful protest – essential part of British life, but that’s not dressing up in costumes like this and disrupting people’s lives.” On Sunday night, a Home Office spokesperson said: “This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election. “We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020. “But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches.” Explore more on these topics Portsmouth Far right Immigration and asylum news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://english.republika.mk/world/the-b.text: Viktor Orban is no longer at the helm of the Hungarian government, but some of the policies that have defended Budapest’s position on migration for years remain even after the change of government. The most visible symbol is the fence on the southern border. Although the new Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced changes in relations with the European Union and a different approach to some foreign policy, he made it clear before taking office that Hungary would remain strict on illegal migration and that the border fence would remain. This is perhaps the most interesting paradox of the political change in Budapest. What was one of Orban’s most criticized policies for years cannot simply be erased today. Under Orban, Hungary erected a physical barrier along its southern border in 2015, during the period of the great migrant crisis in Europe. At the time, Budapest was heavily criticized by some European politicians for its decision to close the border to illegal crossings. Orban, however, has insisted for years that protecting the national border is the state’s first obligation. Today, after the change of government, the fence remains. Even in the new political context, the Hungarian government continues to oppose the mandatory distribution of migrants among EU member states. In 2026, Budapest once again announced that it would not accept the European migration pact in its current form. This is precisely where you can see how deeply migration policy has become embedded in Hungarian politics. Magyar came to power with a promise of change after 16 years of Orbán’s rule, but even his government must take into account the reality of the Hungarian border and the attitude of a significant part of Hungarian society. The new government wants better relations with Brussels and a different approach to the European Union, but when it comes to illegal migration, the space for a complete turnaround is much smaller. And that is precisely why Orbán’s legacy on this issue is perhaps stronger than it seemed after his election defeat. It is even more certain that the European debate on migration today looks different than it did in 2015. Policies to protect external borders, limit illegal crossings and increase control over migration are increasingly part of the European political agenda. What Orban has been pushing for alone for years is now being considered by other European governments. That is why the story of Hungary is not just a story of the fall of a long-serving prime minister. It is also a story of how a policy can survive a political defeat. Orban lost power, but his border policy did not disappear with him. https://wtov9.com/news/local/northern-pa.text: Donors who helped raise more than $23,000 for disabled veterans were recognized at an event hosted by the Northern Panhandle American Legion Riders. Officials said some supporters gave as much as $5,000 toward the cause. “This is going to help soldiers, sailors, airmen that come back with scars that you don't see. And these dogs really help them out,” said Charlie Poland, vice commander of the Northern Panhandle American Legion Riders. Poland said the fundraising total will support multiple service dog teams locally. “One trainer, one dog, one veteran is one team. We raised enough money to support seven service dog teams in our area,” he said. The money will go toward providing service dogs and training at no cost to disabled veterans.

Composite: Brendan Moran/Sportsfile via Getty Images/Getty Images Donald Trump Jr Republican calls for Senate investigation of Trump Jr wedding paid for by Russian oligarch Putin ally helped cover cost of renting private island in the Bahamas for wedding of Trump Jr and Bettina Anderson US politics live – latest updates Joseph Gedeon in Washington Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.15 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 11.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Republican senator has accused Donald Trump Jr of corruption and demanded a Senate investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of his recent wedding in the Bahamas. John Curtis, of Utah, wrote to the leaders of the US Senate judiciary committee on Tuesday, urging them to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals, gifts he has received – and any occasions where his connection to his father, Donald Trump , “was invoked or understood to provide value”. Trump Jr’s wedding warrants the kind of scrutiny Republicans once trained on Hunter Biden, the son of Joe Biden, Curtis said. “A toaster is a wedding gift. A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else,” he wrote in a social media post accompanying the letter to the committee. “Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden’s foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now.” The push follows reporting by ProPublica that Umar Kremlev, the Russian boxing official with close ties to Vladimir Putin, helped cover the cost of renting a private island and staging a fireworks display for the wedding of Trump Jr and Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas in May. Bettina Trump later described Kremlev on Instagram as a “dear friend” who had generously hosted two nights of post-wedding celebrations. Donald Trump, who did not attend the ceremony, defended Kremlev’s involvement but said he was told by Trump Jr that the money would eventually be reimbursed, though explained that giving a wedding party as a gift is “totally allowed” and is also “very common”. It is not the first time Trump Jr’s conduct has drawn scrutiny over ties to Russia. He was a central figure in the Robert Mueller investigation that followed the 2016 election, after it emerged he had attended a Trump Tower meeting with a Russian lawyer who had promised damaging material on Hillary Clinton. The call for a formal committee inquiry marks one of the sharper breaks with the president by a sitting Republican senator. Curtis first flagged the wedding payment as problematic on Friday, calling it “corruption” in a video posted online and promising further comment. He was elected to the Senate in 2024, pledging not to shy away from disagreements with Trump. His letter, addressed to the committee chair, Chuck Grassley of Iowa, and its top Democrat, Dick Durbin of Illinois, lands amid signs of broader unease among Republicans over Trump’s standing heading into November’s US midterm elections, with the party facing pressure over the war in Iran, high gas prices and slipping poll numbers. Republicans in the House of Representatives spent much of 2023 and 2024 investigating whether Hunter Biden traded on his father’s name in his overseas business dealings, an effort that produced a report alleging a conspiracy to enrich the Biden family, but never resulted in impeachment articles reaching a House vote. The Bidens denied wrongdoing throughout. “‘Trust us’ was not enough then,” wrote Curtis, “and it is not enough now.” Explore more on these topics Donald Trump Jr US politics Republicans US political financing Trump-Russia investigation Donald Trump Trump administration news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
